persona.name: Saroja Krishnan
persona.background: She works long hours doing repetitive hand work (harvesting, milking, carrying loads) and has found early-morning tasks increasingly difficult due to hand stiffness.

diagnoses.name: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
diagnoses.description: A chronic inflammatory, potentially crippling arthritis with multisystem involvement; typically symmetric small-joint (MCP/PIP/MTP) involvement with morning stiffness >1 hour and DIP sparing.

diagnoses.name: Osteoarthritis (OA)
diagnoses.description: A noninflammatory degenerative arthritis, usually in older patients; pain worsens with activity, morning stiffness <30 minutes, commonly affects large weight-bearing joints and can involve DIP/PIP while sparing MCP.

diagnoses.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
diagnoses.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease with immune complex formation and complement activation; can have arthritis (typically non-erosive) with features like malar rash, oral ulcers, alopecia, serositis, and renal involvement.

diagnoses.name: Rheumatic fever (rheumatic arthritis)
diagnoses.description: Poststreptococcal illness with acute migratory arthritis mainly affecting major joints; small joints are rarely involved and morning stiffness is not prominent.

diagnoses.name: Palindromic rheumatism
diagnoses.description: Intermittent relapsing and remitting episodes of pain, stiffness and swelling lasting hours to days with symptom-free periods; may progress to rheumatoid arthritis later.

diagnoses.name: Reactive arthritis
diagnoses.description: An inflammatory arthritis often following recent gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection; tends to be asymmetric and oligoarticular and may be associated with conjunctivitis and oral ulcers.

diagnoses.name: Psoriatic arthritis
diagnoses.description: An inflammatory arthritis that may be mono- or polyarticular and symmetric or asymmetric; associated with psoriatic skin and nail changes and can show enthesitis or dactylitis.

diagnoses.name: Gout
diagnoses.description: A crystal-induced arthritis with sudden onset joint pain, redness and swelling, often recurrent; diagnosis is supported by crystal identification on polarized microscopy.

diagnoses.name: Fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS)
diagnoses.description: Chronic widespread pain for >3 months above and below the waist; physical exam is normal except for multiple tender points (classically ≥11/18).

diagnoses.name: Ankylosing spondylitis
diagnoses.description: A chronic inflammatory disorder primarily affecting the axial skeleton (sacroiliac joints and spine) with inflammatory back pain >3 months, morning stiffness improving with activity and worse with rest.

initialComplaint: “For the past few months, my hands and wrists feel stiff and swollen when I wake up. It takes more than an hour before I can brush my teeth or comb my hair properly.”
medicalHistory: No documented prior joint disease. No known history provided of psoriasis, recent gastrointestinal/genitourinary infection, or chronic infections. Medication history not provided.
symptoms:
Subacute/chronic joint pain, swelling and stiffness with morning stiffness lasting >1 hour. Symptoms are symmetric and begin in small joints of the hands (metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints) and wrists; routine early-morning activities like brushing teeth and combing hair are difficult. She reports generalized fatigue and weakness consistent with constitutional features of RA. She notices swelling of the fingers with early spindling (swelling of proximal but not distal interphalangeal joints), with distal interphalangeal joints spared.

relevantFindings:
Joint exam: swollen, warm, tender small joints in a symmetric distribution, predominantly MCP and PIP joints and wrists; DIP joints are spared. Labs (consistent with RA work-up): raised ESR/CRP as acute phase reactants; normocytic normochromic anemia of chronic disease; thrombocytosis may be present. redHerrings: Intermittent episodes of joint swelling could suggest palindromic rheumatism (intermittent arthritis). Generalized pain and fatigue could suggest fibromyalgia syndrome (though FMS exam would be normal except tender points). If she later reports oral ulcers or rash, SLE would enter the differential (SLE can have arthritis with mucocutaneous features). If she reports a recent GI/GU infection with conjunctivitis/oral ulcers, reactive arthritis would become plausible. If she reports sudden attacks of a single joint with marked redness/swelling, gout/pseudogout would be considered (crystals on polarized microscopy).

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about morning stiffness duration and whether it lasts >1 hour
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour is characteristic of RA and helps distinguish inflammatory arthritis from noninflammatory causes.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Morning stiffness lasting >1 hour, with difficulty doing early morning activities (e.g., brushing teeth, combing hair)
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Stiffness dominating in the mornings (‘morning stiffness’) lasting more than 1 hour is characteristic.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask which joints are involved and whether the pattern is symmetric, focusing on small joints (MCP, PIP, MTP) and wrists
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: RA typically begins in small synovial joints with symmetric distribution; this joint pattern supports RA over OA and other arthritides.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Symmetric pain/swelling in MCP, PIP, MTP joints and/or wrists; progression to larger joints may occur later
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “RA can affect any of the synovial (diarthrodial) joints and involvement is usually in a symmetric distribution. Most commonly, RA starts in the small joints, namely metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints…”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about onset pattern: slow/insidious vs acute vs palindromic (relapsing-remitting episodes lasting hours to days)
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: The textbook describes multiple RA onset patterns; identifying palindromic or acute onset supports RA spectrum presentations and guides reassessment if early/atypical.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Slow insidious systemic symptoms preceding arthritis, or acute onset with morning stiffness/polyarthritis/pitting edema, or palindromic relapsing-remitting attacks
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “The onset varies: Slow and insidious… Acute onset… Palindromic onset… relapsing and remitting episodes… alternating with symptom-free periods.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever) and other extra-articular symptoms
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: RA is a systemic disease; constitutional features and extra-articular involvement support inflammatory systemic arthritis and help assess severity.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever (<38°C) and/or symptoms suggesting extra-articular involvement
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “RA is a systemic disease and features such as fatigue, weight loss, and low-grade fever (<38°C) occur frequently.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about symptoms suggesting specific extra-articular joint involvement: hoarseness/stridor (cricoarytenoid) and neck symptoms suggestive of cervical spine involvement
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: The textbook notes clinically important non-peripheral joint involvement (cricoarytenoid and cervical spine) that can occur in RA and indicates broader disease.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Hoarseness of voice and/or inspiratory stridor; symptoms concerning for cervical spine involvement
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Cricoarytenoid joint involvement may present (30%) with hoarseness of voice and inspiratory stridor.” / “the cervical spine (atlantoaxial subluxation) can be involved producing quadriparesis.”

keyExaminations.action: Examine hands/wrists/feet for synovitis: palpate joint capsules for synovial thickening, soft-tissue swelling and effusions; assess warmth, tenderness, swelling
keyExaminations.reasoning: Inflammatory arthritis is defined by clinical inflammation; RA commonly affects small joints and produces synovial thickening and swelling.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Swollen, warm, tender joints with synovial thickening/effusion in a symmetric small-joint distribution (MCP/PIP/MTP, wrists)
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Erythema, warmth, pain and swelling are the cardinal features of inflammation… Palpate the joint capsule for synovial thickening, soft tissue swelling effusions.”

keyExaminations.action: Assess for characteristic rheumatoid hand findings and joint sparing pattern (DIP sparing) and look for early ‘spindling’ of fingers
keyExaminations.reasoning: The textbook highlights DIP sparing and early spindling as characteristic hand findings in RA, helping differentiate from OA and other arthritides.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Spindling of fingers (PIP swelling with DIP spared); DIP joints typically spared unless coexistent OA
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “The DIP joint is characteristically always spared… Spindling of the fingers: It is the earliest finding characterized by swelling of the proximal, but not the distal interphalangeal joints.”

keyExaminations.action: Inspect for chronic deformities (ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière) and document symmetry
keyExaminations.reasoning: Chronic RA can cause irreversible deformities; documenting these supports established RA and correlates with radiographic changes.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Ulnar deviation and/or swan-neck/boutonnière deformities with symmetrical distribution
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Deformities… Ulnar deviation… ‘Swan-neck’ deformity…” / “Deformities… with symmetrical distribution.”

keyExaminations.action: Examine for rheumatoid nodules on extensor surfaces and areas subject to repeated trauma
keyExaminations.reasoning: Rheumatoid nodules are a classic extra-articular manifestation and are strongly associated with seropositive RA and more severe disease.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Firm, nontender subcutaneous nodules (2 mm to 5 cm) on extensor surfaces (e.g., forearms) or other listed sites
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Nodules are seen in about one-fourth of patients with RA and, almost exclusively in those patients who are seropositive for rheumatoid factor… Typically occur on extensor surfaces…”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: CBC provides diagnostic clues in inflammatory arthritides and RA (anemia of chronic disease, thrombocytosis, variable WBC).
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Normocytic normochromic anemia (anemia of chronic disease) and/or thrombocytosis; WBC may be raised/normal/low (Felty’s syndrome)
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “A complete blood count… may provide diagnostic clues.” / “Anemia of chronic disease is seen in majority of patients… Thrombocytosis is common… WBC counts may be raised, normal, or profoundly depressed (Felty’s syndrome).”

keyInvestigations.action: Order inflammatory markers: ESR and/or C-reactive protein (CRP)
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Acute phase reactants parallel RA disease activity and persistent elevation carries poor prognosis; also supports inflammatory arthritis.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Elevated ESR and/or CRP consistent with active inflammatory arthritis
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Acute phase reactants, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels parallel the activity of the disease…”

keyInvestigations.action: Order serology: Rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA)
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Textbook lists RF and ACPA as key serologies for RA; also notes interpretation caution for RF.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Positive RF and/or ACPA (seropositivity supports RA; dual positivity associated with more systemic features)
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Serology: Rheumatoid factor… Anticyclic citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA).” / “Rheumatoid factor lacks sensitivity and specificity; hence both positive and negative results should be interpreted cautiously.”

keyInvestigations.action: Order plain radiographs (X-rays) of affected joints (hands/feet/wrists as appropriate)
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Radiographs show characteristic RA changes and help document structural disease (erosions, joint space narrowing, periarticular osteoporosis) with symmetric pattern.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Symmetrical involvement with juxta-articular osteoporosis, soft tissue swelling, marginal erosions, and joint space narrowing (ABCDE’S mnemonic)
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Radiographs… symmetrical pattern of involvement, juxta-articular osteoporosis, soft tissue swelling, bone erosions and narrowing of the joint space.”

keyInvestigations.action: If needed for early disease or to assess persistent synovitis, order ultrasonography (including Doppler) and/or MRI
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Ultrasound/MRI are more sensitive than plain radiographs for early synovitis and soft-tissue disease; Doppler helps demonstrate persistent synovitis when deciding on DMARD need or efficacy.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Synovitis detected before radiographic joint damage; Doppler evidence of persistent synovitis
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Ultrasonography and MRI: More sensitive than plain radiographs and detects soft-tissue synovitis before joint damage. Doppler ultrasound is useful for demonstration persistent synovitis…”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Osteoarthritis (OA)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: OA is typically noninflammatory with morning stiffness <30 minutes, pain worsened with movement/activity, often asymmetrical, and commonly involves DIP joints with sparing of MCP; RA typically has morning stiffness >1 hour, symmetric small-joint (MCP/PIP) involvement and spares DIP.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Morning stiffness for >1 hour” (RA) vs “Morning stiffness for <30 minutes” (OA) / “Osteoarthritis involves distal interphalangeal (DIP)… with sparing of metacarpophalangeal joints. Rheumatoid arthritis spares DIP but affects PIP and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Psoriatic arthritis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Consider if there are psoriatic skin and nail changes; joint pattern may involve DIP as well (unlike RA which spares DIP).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Psoriatic skin and nail changes accompany psoriatic arthritis.” / “Psoriasis and crystal arthropathies affect all three joints [DIP, PIP, MCP].”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Reactive arthritis / spondyloarthropathies
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Reactive arthritis and spondyloarthropathies tend to be asymmetric and oligoarticular, often affecting lower extremities; reactive arthritis suggested by recent GI/GU infection with conjunctivitis and oral ulcers; spondyloarthropathies may present with enthesitis/dactylitis and back disease (axial involvement).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Joint involvement in RA tends to be symmetrical and polyarticular whereas spondyloarthropathy… reactive arthritis involvement is asymmetric and oligoarticular.” / “Reactive arthritis is suggested by a history of recent gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, conjunctivitis and oral ulcers.” / “Spondyloarthropathies can present with enthesitis or dactylitis…”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Crystal-induced arthritis (gout/pseudogout) or infectious arthritis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: These are often mono- or oligoarticular. If suspected, perform synovial fluid analysis: crystals suggest gout/pseudogout; WBC >50,000/mm3 suggests infection and requires culture. RA synovial fluid typically has WBC 5000–50,000/µL with neutrophil predominance and no crystals/organisms.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Crystal and infectious arthritides are often mono or oligoarticular whereas OA and RA are polyarticular.” / “WBC count higher than 50,000 per mm3 indicates infection… synovial fluid needs to be cultured…” / “Synovial fluid… 5000–50,000 per microliter… neutrophils with no crystals or organism.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Systematically confirm inflammatory, symmetric small-joint arthritis with morning stiffness >1 hour and objective synovitis on examination (warmth, swelling, tenderness, synovial thickening/effusion), noting typical joint distribution (MCP/PIP/MTP, wrists) and DIP sparing. Screen for constitutional and extra-articular features (e.g., rheumatoid nodules; hoarseness/stridor; cervical spine involvement). Order cost-effective tests first (CBC, ESR/CRP), then RA serology (RF and ACPA, interpreting RF cautiously), followed by radiographs of affected joints for characteristic changes (symmetry, juxta-articular osteoporosis, erosions, joint space narrowing). Use ultrasound (Doppler) or MRI when early disease is suspected or to demonstrate persistent synovitis and assess treatment efficacy. Reconsider alternative diagnoses particularly with asymmetric arthritis, migrating pattern, predominantly large-joint arthritis, DIP involvement, rashes, back disease, renal disease, leukopenia, or hypocomplementemia.

precomputedExplanations.description: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, systemic **autoimmune inflammatory arthritis** characterized by persistent **synovitis** leading to pain, swelling, and progressive joint damage. It classically presents with **symmetric** involvement of small joints (especially **MCP/PIP** and wrists) and prolonged **morning stiffness**, with potential constitutional and extra-articular manifestations.
keySymptoms: **Morning stiffness >1 hour** - Suggests inflammatory arthritis; prolonged stiffness is typical of RA over osteoarthritis.
**Symmetric small-joint pain/swelling** - RA characteristically affects both hands with symmetric **MCP/PIP** and wrist synovitis.
**MCP and PIP involvement** - Early RA commonly begins in these joints due to prominent synovial inflammation.
**Wrist involvement** - Frequent early site in RA; supports inflammatory polyarthritis rather than isolated degenerative disease.
**DIP sparing** - Helps distinguish RA from osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis, which often involve DIP joints.
**Difficulty with early-morning activities** - Functional limitation on waking reflects active synovitis and inflammatory stiffness.
**Fatigue and weakness** - Constitutional symptoms reflect systemic inflammation and cytokine-mediated effects in RA.
**Spindling of fingers** - Fusiform PIP swelling indicates synovial hypertrophy/effusion typical of RA.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This 42-year-old woman has subacute-to-chronic **symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis** with prominent **morning stiffness lasting >1 hour**, strongly favoring RA. The distribution (predominant **MCP/PIP** and wrists) with **DIP sparing** is classic for RA and matches her functional difficulty with brushing teeth and combing hair on waking. Expected supportive findings include elevated **ESR/CRP**, possible **normocytic normochromic anemia of chronic disease** and **thrombocytosis**, and seropositivity for **RF** and/or **ACPA**. Imaging and synovial fluid features (periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, inflammatory WBC without crystals/organisms) further align with RA pathophysiology involving **B cells**, **CD4+ T cells**, and **complement-mediated immune activation**.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Osteoarthritis (OA)** is a degenerative joint disease driven by progressive **articular cartilage loss** with secondary **subchondral bone remodeling**. It typically causes **mechanical pain** that worsens with use and improves with rest, with minimal systemic inflammation.
keySymptoms: **Mechanical joint pain** - Pain worsens with activity and improves with rest; inflammatory features are limited.
**Brief morning stiffness** - Stiffness usually lasts <30 minutes, improving quickly after movement.
**Bony enlargement** - Osteophyte-related enlargement (e.g., Heberden/Bouchard nodes) rather than soft synovitis.
**Crepitus** - Grating sensation with joint motion due to irregular cartilage and osteophytes.
**Functional limitation** - Reduced range of motion and difficulty with weight-bearing tasks as disease progresses.
**Common joint distribution** - Often affects knees/hips/spine and hands at DIP/1st CMC more than MCP.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: Although hand symptoms can occur in **OA**, the typical pattern is **DIP** and **1st CMC** involvement with **short-lived morning stiffness** and little true synovitis. OA is generally a **non-systemic** condition, so prominent **fatigue** and elevated **ESR/CRP** are less characteristic. Imaging in OA classically shows **non-uniform joint space narrowing**, **osteophytes**, and **subchondral sclerosis**, rather than early periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient has **>1 hour morning stiffness**, **symmetric MCP/PIP and wrist synovitis**, and **DIP sparing**, which is classic for **rheumatoid arthritis** rather than OA. Her constitutional symptoms and inflammatory labs (raised **ESR/CRP**, anemia of chronic disease, possible thrombocytosis) also favor **inflammatory arthritis**, not OA.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Morning stiffness duration** - OA: typically <30 minutes; RA: often >60 minutes with marked morning disability.
**Joint distribution (hands)** - OA: **DIP** and **1st CMC** commonly; RA: **MCP/PIP** and wrists, usually **DIP spared**.
**Nature of swelling** - OA: bony enlargement/osteophytes; RA: **soft, warm, tender synovitis** with spindling.
**Systemic features** - OA: absent; RA: **fatigue**, malaise, and other constitutional symptoms can occur.
**Inflammatory markers** - OA: usually normal ESR/CRP; RA: frequently elevated **ESR/CRP**.
**Radiographic pattern** - OA: osteophytes, **subchondral sclerosis**, non-uniform narrowing; RA: **periarticular osteopenia**, uniform narrowing, **marginal erosions**.
missingFindings: **DIP joint involvement** - OA commonly affects DIP joints; this case explicitly shows **DIP sparing**.
**Osteophytes/Heberden nodes** - Typical OA bony nodal changes are not described on exam.
**Non-uniform joint space narrowing** - OA classically shows asymmetric/non-uniform narrowing; case suggests RA-type changes.
**Subchondral sclerosis** - A hallmark of OA imaging; not reported and RA features are more consistent.

precomputedExplanations.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, multisystem autoimmune disease driven by immune complex formation and complement activation. It commonly affects skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, and serosal membranes, with symptoms that fluctuate in flares and remissions.
keySymptoms: **Arthralgia/arthritis** - Joint pain with inflammatory features; usually non-erosive and often intermittent in flares.
**Photosensitivity** - Sun exposure provokes rash or systemic symptoms due to immune-mediated skin inflammation.
**Malar rash** - Fixed erythema over cheeks and nasal bridge, typically sparing nasolabial folds.
**Oral/nasal ulcers** - Painless mucosal ulcers reflecting immune-mediated epithelial injury during active disease.
**Serositis** - Pleuritis or pericarditis causing sharp chest pain, often worse with breathing or lying flat.
**Renal involvement** - Proteinuria or hematuria from lupus nephritis due to immune complex glomerulonephritis.
**Cytopenias** - Hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia from autoimmune destruction or marrow suppression.
**Raynaud phenomenon** - Episodic digital color changes from vasospasm, often triggered by cold or stress.

SLE can cause inflammatory joint symptoms, but lupus arthritis is typically **non-erosive**, less characterized by persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis with classic RA distribution, and is usually accompanied by systemic features such as **photosensitive rash**, **oral ulcers**, **serositis**, or **renal** findings. The provided work-up pattern (elevated **ESR/CRP**, possible **RF/ACPA positivity**, and radiographic **marginal erosions/juxta-articular osteopenia**) aligns with RA rather than SLE.

precomputedExplanations.description: Acute rheumatic fever is a post–**Group A Streptococcus** immune-mediated inflammatory disease that can affect joints, heart, skin, and CNS. precomputedExplanations.description: Palindromic rheumatism is an episodic inflammatory arthritis characterized by sudden, recurrent attacks of joint pain and swelling with complete resolution between episodes. It may precede or evolve into **rheumatoid arthritis (RA)**, but by definition does not cause persistent synovitis or progressive erosive damage during symptom-free intervals.
keySymptoms: **Recurrent self-limited attacks** - Sudden flares of mono- or oligoarthritis lasting hours to days, then fully resolve.
**Complete intercritical recovery** - No persistent joint swelling or stiffness between attacks; function returns to baseline.
**Migratory joint involvement** - Different joints may be affected in different episodes rather than fixed symmetric pattern.
**Periarticular soft-tissue swelling** - Swelling may involve tendons or periarticular tissues, not only synovium.
**Variable serology** - **RF** and **ACPA** can be positive, but diagnosis is primarily clinical and episodic.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has chronic, persistent inflammatory small-joint synovitis with **symmetric** involvement of **MCP**, **PIP**, and **wrists**, plus **morning stiffness >1 hour** and constitutional symptoms (fatigue/weakness). The pattern (small joints, symmetric distribution, **DIP sparing**, early spindling) is classic for **rheumatoid arthritis (RA)** rather than an episodic syndrome. Supporting work-up features described for this case (raised **ESR/CRP**, anemia of chronic disease, possible thrombocytosis, **RF/ACPA** positivity, and radiographic **juxta-articular osteopenia/marginal erosions**) align with established RA pathophysiology and progression. Palindromic rheumatism would require discrete attacks with complete resolution and typically lacks persistent exam and imaging changes.

The exam/imaging/lab profile described (persistent symmetric synovitis with inflammatory markers and possible erosive changes) is much more consistent with **RA** than a purely episodic condition.
